# Execution Boundary Principles {.unnumbered}

Part III governs the dangerous boundary where non-deterministic models interact with deterministic external software and real-world environments. Because language models lack hardware separation between instructions and data, execution runtimes must enforce least-privilege virtualization, typed ABIs, deterministic verification gates, and compensating Sagas.

::: {#pri-vol3-strict-abi .callout-principle title="The Strict Action ABI"}

**Invariant**: Stochastic models must interface with deterministic environments through typed, schema-validated, grammar-constrained, and idempotent protocol contracts.

**Implication**: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes wire formats but provides zero privilege ring isolation; schemas must not be confused with security boundaries.

:::

::: {#pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing .callout-principle title="Zero-Trust Sandboxing"}

**Invariant**: Because language models lack hardware separation between instructions and data (W⊕X failure), execution runtimes must assume policy compromise and isolate side-effects inside ephemeral protection domains.

**Implication**: Prompt guardrails cannot stop indirect injection; security must be enforced by hardware virtualization (MicroVMs) and network egress proxies.

:::

::: {#pri-vol3-reversibility-boundary .callout-principle title="The Reversibility Boundary"}

**Invariant**: Internal state is private and reversible; external state is shared and often irreversible. Failure recovery requires distributed Sagas with deterministic compensating actions.

**Implication**: Language models cannot reliably generate their own rollbacks; recovery from failed external mutations requires deterministic compensating scripts.

:::
